Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Reconstructing the in vivo dynamics of hematopoietic stem cells from telomere length distributions" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Naama Barkai (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.. The manuscript has been significantly improved and the points of the referees have been taken into account. There is one technical comment of referee two that the authors should consider before acceptance, as outlined below. The new Figure 2—figure supplement 1 clarifying the difference between the two models is very useful and might be well suited as a main figure.

Reviewer #1:

The authors have carefully addressed the reviewer comments. The issues raised in my first report have been clarified and the text is now much clearer.

Reviewer #2:

In revised version of their manuscript "Reconstructing the in vivo dynamics of hematopoietic stem cells from telomere length distributions", the authors have incorporated the comments and suggestions of the three reviewers, increasing the quality of the manuscript considerably. Especially some confusion due to inconsistent nomenclature has been sorted out and makes the manuscript much easier to read.

In particular, the authors responded to all my concerns/issues and could sort out most of them. However, I would like to comment on some specific points and ask for additional clarification if possible.

Fitting procedure:

I have the feeling that it is a bit confusing/redundant now; to summarize this is what I found as fitting setup:

1) You fit your models in the section "In vivo measurements of telomere length…" giving some parameter estimates;

2) You perform ABC-rejection sampling in the next section, giving some idea about the posterior parameter distribution and uncertainties;

3) You do maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters (+ confidence intervals), again giving some idea about the uncertainties.

So, you fit the same data, with three different methods (actually I'm not sure what the difference between 1 and 3 is). This seems unnecessary and confusing. Why doing basically the same thing three times? Is this for different models, or for comparison? What’s the difference between 1 and 3?

One observes that the estimates a (slightly) different, e.g. telomere_loss_ABC = 0.071 vs telormere_loss_MLE=0.075. Is this difference due to the different "error measure", i.e. R2 for ABC and quadratic distance/Gaussian error for MLE? Since you do ABC to get a handle on the uncertainties, you should report them (as you did for the MLE), i.e. the boundaries of the credibility intervals.

One major advantage of having the full posterior is that you can look at correlations of parameters. The one-dimensional confidence/credibility intervals (or an approximation) you can also obtain from MLE. Consider showing e.g. pairwise scatter-plots of the posterior samples to show whether there are some correlations/dependencies.

This whole subject discussed above should be straightened out in the final manuscript. Choose one suitable method and stick to it (I would suggest MCMC + Bayes factors, which gives you posterior uncertainties and model comparison or the ABC version). Otherwise the reader will get lost.

Model selection:

Thanks for incorporating some model selection. Any particular reason why you choose AIC and not BIC? Does the BIC select the same model? Since the multiphase model is inferior to model 2, you should be careful not to interpret this model too much.

Figure 2:

Thanks for showing the fits in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. This helps a lot to see why model 1 doesn't explain the data so well. Is there any reason not to put this figure into the main manuscript (instead of the old Figure 2 which doesn't show the linear fit)?

About my question on exponential waiting times:

My question was about cell cycle times, i.e. the time from a cell's "birth" (the division of its mother cell) until it divides. From what I understood when reading the supplement section "Connections to the Normal and Lognormal distribution", you look at the "distribution" N(i)(t), i.e. the number of cells across states, which is Poisson (model 1) or generalized Poisson (model 2). These can then be approximated by normals/lognormals.

However, to me this is fundamentally different from a normal/lognormally distributed cell cycle time. The cell cycle time tells us when a single cell is going to divide. Your N(i)(t) tells us how a population of states spreads over the states i. I don't see an immediate connection between those to quantities. Please comment on that.

Reviewer #3:

The authors have addressed all of my comments and improved the manuscript accordingly. I think it should be accepted for publication in the current form.

results.result: The mathematical model predicts that telomere length distributions form a traveling wave that contains information about progressive telomere loss and the fraction of symmetric cell divisions. Under symmetric stem cell self-renewal, the model predicts logarithmic decay of average telomere length with age, while asymmetric divisions alone produce linear decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C25, and C27 describe core mathematical predictions that are internally consistent and derived from the differential equations presented. The traveling wave behavior and logarithmic vs. linear decay patterns are mathematically sound predictions that follow from the model assumptions and are later tested against experimental data.

results.result: The study collected telomere length data from 356 healthy individuals aged 0-85 years, including 47 cord blood samples and 28 bone marrow biopsies from Hodgkin lymphoma patients without bone marrow involvement. Average telomere length was measured using Flow-FISH in all samples, and 66 samples were additionally analyzed with Q-FISH to obtain full telomere length distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C28-C31, and C53-C57 consistently describe the sample collection, methodology, and ethical approval. The use of established Flow-FISH and Q-FISH protocols with appropriate citations supports the validity of the measurements. The use of Hodgkin lymphoma patients without bone marrow involvement as healthy controls is reasonable but could introduce subtle confounding factors.

results.result: Analysis of telomere length data reveals an expanding stem cell pool during childhood and adolescence (with approximately 30-35% symmetric divisions population-wide), followed by an approximately maintained stem cell population in adults (with 0-20% symmetric divisions). Bayesian analysis suggests transitions in stem cell dynamics occur between ages 6-7 years for lymphocytes and 10-15 years for granulocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C38-C42 present a coherent picture supported by multiple analytical approaches (maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian inference, and model selection via AIC). The findings are validated on an independent dataset of 835 individuals (C37), strengthening confidence. The transition ages and probability estimates are derived from rigorous statistical methods with appropriate uncertainty quantification.

results.result: Model 1 (asymmetric divisions only) fails to explain the accelerated telomere loss in infants, underestimating initial telomere length. Model 2 (incorporating symmetric divisions) provides superior fit with parameter estimates of 75±7 bp/year loss for lymphocytes (p=0.35±0.07) and 68±5 bp/year for granulocytes (p=0.44±0.2). Model selection via AIC strongly favors Model 2 over Model 1 and multiphase models.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 and C43 present a clear model comparison with quantitative parameter estimates and statistical model selection. The AIC values (Model 1: 2550, Model 2: 2328, multiphase: 2361) provide strong statistical evidence favoring Model 2. The parameter estimates include confidence intervals and are validated on independent data (C37), supporting the conclusions.

results.result: The method can detect individual differences in stem cell dynamics from single tissue samples. Individual analysis of 66 samples reveals low symmetric self-renewal probability (p=0.005-0.03) in adults and substantial inter-individual variation in telomere loss rates (18-110 bp/year).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C45, and C46 describe individual-level analysis that complements population-level findings. The individual parameter estimates are consistent with population-level results (C39, C42), providing internal validation. The wide range of telomere loss rates (18-110 bp/year) reflects genuine biological variation, though quality of individual fits should be assessed (mentioned in Supplementary file 1 but not fully evaluated here).

results.result: Telomere loss rates differ between cell lineages and change with age: granulocytes show decreasing loss rates (-0.78 bp/year with age), lymphocytes show slightly increasing rates (+0.27 bp/year), and bone marrow shows intermediate decreasing rates (-0.36 bp/year). This pattern is consistent with age-related myeloid skewing of hematopoietic stem cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 describe lineage-specific differences supported by individual sample analysis (Figure 7) and consistent with cited prior work on myeloid skewing (C49). The quantitative rates are derived from data, though the manuscript notes these trends are likely non-linear. The biological interpretation linking reduced granulocyte telomere loss to increased myeloid progenitor pools is plausible and supported by citation.

results.result: Assuming 50 bp telomere loss per cell division implies approximately 1 hematopoietic stem cell replication per year in adults.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 presents a straightforward calculation combining the measured population-level telomere loss rate (~50 bp/year in adults) with established knowledge about per-division telomere loss (50 bp, cited from Rufer et al., 1999). This inference is mathematically sound and consistent with prior observations of rare stem cell turnover under homeostasis.

results.result: The manuscript establishes biological background on stem cell biology, telomere structure and function, and the rationale for using telomere length as a biomarker of stem cell proliferation history. Key assumptions include that mature cell telomere distributions proxy stem cell distributions and that average telomere length shortens by a constant factor per division.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C23 present established biological knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The key modeling assumption (C23) that mature cell telomere distributions proxy stem cell distributions is supported by citation and is reasonable given constant differentiation divisions (C22). However, the model's use of average telomere length (C19) rather than shortest telomere (C20) is acknowledged as a potential limitation that may underestimate senescent cells.

results.result: An independent dataset of 835 healthy humans from Aubert et al. (2012) confirms the parameter estimations and the accelerated telomere loss during adolescence.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 describes external validation on a large independent dataset that confirms the key findings. This substantially strengthens confidence in the results, as the patterns are reproducible across different cohorts and measurement protocols. The validation specifically confirms the accelerated adolescent telomere loss, a key prediction distinguishing Model 2 from Model 1.
